description: Glute bridge guide: lift your hips to build glutes and hamstrings that support the pelvis, how it should feel, mistakes, easier and harder versions.
intro: The glute bridge strengthens the glutes and hamstrings around the back of the pelvis. It does not train the pelvic floor directly, but strong hips support the pelvis, and a gentle Kegel as you lift links the two.
feel: You should feel your buttocks and the back of your thighs working, with a line from knees to shoulders at the top. Your lower back feels neutral, not pinched. Watch for breath holding, pressing your head down or hamstring cramps. If you feel it mostly in your lower back, lift a little lower and squeeze your glutes more.

mistakes.right: Press through your heels. If your hamstrings cramp, bring your feet a little closer to your hips.
Keep knees in line with hips and feet on the way up and down.
Lower slowly, one vertebra at a time, and relax fully at the bottom.

easier: Lift only halfway, or do fewer reps with a short rest between each.
harder: Hold the top for 3 to 5 seconds, slow the lowering, or move on to the bridge march or single-leg bridge.
who: Desk workers with weak or stiff hips, beginners, and people over 40 who want hip strength for daily movement.
skip: Modify or skip after recent back, hip or abdominal surgery, with a hernia, or if back pain worsens with the lift. In later pregnancy, lying flat may be uncomfortable, so ask your doctor or physiotherapist. Stop if it hurts.

faq.q: Do glute bridges strengthen the pelvic floor?
faq.a: Bridges mainly work the glutes and hamstrings. The pelvic floor joins in a little, and you can add a gentle Kegel at the top, but keep doing Kegels too.

faq.q: Why do I feel bridges in my lower back?
faq.a: Usually the back arches at the top or the glutes are not doing enough. Keep your ribs down, lift a little lower and squeeze your buttocks.
